article_content: A Russian weight-loss group, 'Get Thin Like Me', faced significant backlash for suggesting a ‘blockade diet’ to its followers. This diet, mimicking the meager rations endured during the Siege of Leningrad, was presented as a way to ‘honor’ World War II veterans.  The Siege of Leningrad, a nearly 2.5-year Nazi siege, tragically resulted in the starvation deaths of an estimated 630,000 people in what is now St. Petersburg. The insensitive ‘blockade diet’ suggestion appeared on the group's Facebook page, coinciding with the 71st anniversary of the city's liberation.  The post, according to The Moscow Times, urged followers to ‘watch your figure and commemorate the Leningrad siege at the same time,’ outlining a daily intake similar to factory workers in December 1941: 400 grams of bread and unlimited water, with men allowed 100 grams of vodka instead of bread. The group even provided a recipe for ‘blockade bread,’ including ingredients only available in pet shops. The suffering during the siege was extreme. Food scarcity led residents to consume pets, dirt, glue, and in some cases, engage in cannibalism. Streets were littered with bodies, as survivors lacked the strength to bury the deceased.  The post sparked widespread criticism, with many Facebook users condemning the group's insensitivity and disrespect for the victims. The Siege of Leningrad, beginning September 8, 1941, subjected nearly 3 million civilians, including 400,000 children, to immense hardship.  The harsh winter of 1941-1942 saw rations plummet to as low as 125 grams of bread per day for white-collar workers, with heating shut off.  By the time the siege ended on January 27, 1944, after 872 days, an estimated 630,000 lives were lost, with some historians estimating the number closer to 800,000.

article_content: A three-year-old girl, Carmen Ellis, died after being taken to the emergency room with bruises and bite marks. Court documents state her last words were, ‘Papa, I hate you.’ Carmen succumbed to her injuries and was taken off life support. Her mother’s boyfriend, Jose Cruz, admitted to losing his temper, beating her repeatedly with a belt, and shaking her. Cruz claimed he ‘blanked out’ after Carmen vomited. Samantha Ellis, Carmen’s mother, told investigators that Cruz prevented her from seeking medical attention sooner. Cruz is charged with murder and is being held in solitary confinement, with a court appearance scheduled for November. Police responded to a call on Tuesday, finding Carmen unresponsive and severely bruised. She was kept alive until Wednesday to donate her organs. Cruz was found in the house wearing a wet T-shirt and acting agitated. A neighbor reported possible bite marks on Carmen’s face in July, but the case was referred to Child Services. Carmen’s grandmother described her as ‘smart and beautiful.’  The mother is not currently facing charges, but the investigation is ongoing.

article_content: Romelu Lukaku has apologized for any offense caused by his comments regarding Nicolas Anelka.  Lukaku, the 20-year-old Belgian striker on loan at Everton from Chelsea, appeared in a video interview on Everton's website. In the interview, he downplayed the significance of Anelka's 'quenelle' celebration, stating that Anelka shouldn't be banned. The 'quenelle,' a pose Anelka made after scoring against West Ham on December 28th, has been deemed anti-Semitic and similar to an inverted Nazi salute. Anelka faces an FA charge, with a response deadline of Thursday at 6 pm.  Lukaku issued a statement through Kick It Out, an anti-discrimination group for which he's an ambassador, clarifying that he was supporting a friend and player he admires.  He apologized for any offense caused, emphasizing that he did not endorse Anelka's gesture. The statement from Kick It Out supported Lukaku's clarification, stating that he had no intention of supporting the gesture and would continue as an ambassador.  Lukaku reaffirmed his commitment to informing young people about the harmful effects of discrimination.  The incident has created significant controversy, with Anelka facing an FA investigation and sponsors threatening to withdraw their support from West Bromwich Albion if Anelka remains with the club. Anelka's 'quenelle' celebration, performed after scoring in West Brom’s 3-3 draw with West Ham on December 28th, 2013, is an inverted Nazi salute created by controversial French comedian Dieudonné M'bala M'bala and has anti-Semitic connotations. The gesture prompted outrage in France, with the sports minister labeling Anelka’s actions 'disgusting'.  The FA's investigation and the subsequent sponsor backlash highlight the serious nature of the incident and the far-reaching consequences of Anelka's actions.

article_content: Cyber Monday is approaching, promising significant online discounts.  Its attractive offers also present hidden risks. Understanding Cyber Monday's impact on shopping habits and finances is crucial before participating.  Retailers fiercely compete, leading to year-low prices on various products.  Discounts aren't limited to older items; they often include the latest electronics and fashion. The scale of these discounts, impacting luxury and everyday items, allows significant savings.  Shopping from anywhere is advantageous, saving time and reducing holiday shopping stress.  Cyber Monday simplifies price comparisons, review reading, and informed decision-making, offering a personalized experience.  Exclusive deals, including price reductions and bundle deals, are often available. Online retailers offer a wider product range than physical stores, including niche items and those from smaller businesses. However, great deals can trigger impulsive buying, exceeding needs and financial capacity.  Aggressive marketing tactics amplify this risk.  Cyber Monday's high online traffic makes it a prime target for scammers, offering fake sites, counterfeit products, and phishing attempts.  Shipping delays and backorders are also significant risks, especially for holiday gifts.  Website crashes during peak traffic can disrupt purchases and compromise security. Before participating, assess your finances and set a budget.  Consider if the items will be on sale and whether the convenience is worth it. Price comparison is essential, as some deals might be misleading.  Compare Cyber Monday with other sales events like Black Friday or post-holiday sales.  Cyber Monday's success depends on individual circumstances and shopping habits. Savvy shoppers who budget effectively can benefit, while others may find better options throughout the year.

article_content: Two Tory MPs claimed last night that the Ministry of Defence is considering controversial proposals to cut hundreds more full-time soldiers.  The regular Army has already been reduced to its weakest strength since before the Napoleonic Wars due to cuts announced earlier this year, with plans to shrink it to 82,000 soldiers by 2015. MPs Patrick Mercer and John Baron, both former Army officers, predict that further reductions are inevitable in 2016 and 2017 due to economic pressures.  Mercer, a former Colonel in the Worcestershire and Sherwood Foresters, believes two infantry and cavalry regiments could be targeted, stating that ‘the cuts will take the regular Army below the currently projected baseline figure of 82,000, which would be hugely damaging.’ Baron, a former Royal Regiment of Fusiliers officer, called plans to reduce full-time soldiers while increasing reservists from 15,000 to 30,000 ‘mistakes.’ The MoD responded by stating that ‘This unhelpful speculation is completely unsubstantiated.’

article_content: The New Year Honours list sparked a controversy after a knighthood was awarded to a Conservative MP who previously claimed expenses for Aga cooker servicing. This ignited further criticism of Prime Minister David Cameron, already accused of cronyism for favoring Conservative donors and friends. The expenses scandal resurfaced, highlighting claims made by several MPs including Peter Luff, who also faced criticism for changing his second home designation and claiming thousands for home renovations and even tea sets.  Kevin Barron, a Labour MP knighted despite past controversial expense claims, and Richard Ottaway, another Tory MP receiving a knighthood, also faced scrutiny. Richard Ottaway’s arrangement of paying the Croydon Conservative Association for office space raised concerns about potential extra funding for party activities. The disproportionate number of knighthoods awarded to male Tory MPs compared to female counterparts fueled additional criticism. Concerns about transparency in the honours process, and the appointment of a former Conservative campaigns officer, Laura Wyld, to oversee public appointments, further intensified the backlash. The knighthood awarded to Paul Tucker, a former Bank of England deputy governor involved in the Libor scandal, also generated controversy. Dame Tessa Jowell advocated for greater transparency in the honours system.

Isso intensificou as críticas ao primeiro-ministro David Cameron, já acusado de nepotismo por favorecer doadores e amigos conservadores. O escândalo de despesas ressurgiu, destacando as reivindicações de vários deputados, incluindo Peter Luff, criticado também por mudar a designação de sua segunda residência e solicitar milhares em reformas e até mesmo jogos de chá.  Kevin Barron, deputado trabalhista condecorado apesar de reivindicações de despesas controversas passadas, e Richard Ottaway, outro deputado conservador condecorado, também foram alvo de escrutínio. O acordo de Richard Ottaway de pagar à Associação Conservadora de Croydon pelo espaço do escritório gerou preocupações sobre um possível financiamento extra para atividades partidárias. O número desproporcional de condecorações a deputados conservadores do sexo masculino em comparação com o feminino gerou críticas adicionais. Preocupações sobre a transparência no processo de honrarias, e a nomeação de uma ex-funcionária de campanhas conservadoras, Laura Wyld, para supervisionar nomeações públicas, intensificaram a reação. A condecoração a Paul Tucker, ex-vice-governador do Banco da Inglaterra envolvido no escândalo do Libor, também gerou controvérsia. Dame Tessa Jowell defendeu maior transparência no sistema de honrarias.

article_content: The Premier League is launching a new European cup competition for Under-21 teams. This season will see English and continental clubs compete. Sportsmail reports that the top eight teams from the U21 Premier League (including Manchester United, Manchester City, and Chelsea), along with eight international teams (including Celtic), will participate in the 16-team tournament.  This initiative is part of the 2011 Elite Player Performance Plan, aiming to improve the standard of young players from top English clubs. Liverpool, last season's U21 runners-up, declined participation, enabling West Ham to join. The competition will run concurrently with a revamped domestic U21 league, featuring promotion and relegation, and will be broadcast by Sky Sports and BT Sport. Organizers anticipate strong attendance and expect clubs to field their best near-first-team players. Schalke's Oliver Ruhnert, a respected youth football expert, supports the initiative, emphasizing exposure to diverse playing styles and international audiences. The format includes four groups of four, followed by two-legged knockout rounds, potentially in the clubs' main stadiums. Three over-21 players per team are permitted.  The competition prioritizes development; there will be no prize money or commercial opportunities in its inaugural season. The name and final venue remain undetermined.

article_content: The wife and three children of fugitive Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi, along with some grandchildren, arrived in Algeria on Monday morning, according to Algerian diplomats. Mourad Benmehidi, Algeria's UN ambassador, informed UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon. Benmehidi stated Algeria granted entry on 'humanitarian grounds' to Safia, Aisha, Hannibal, and Mohamed Gaddafi, and their children. He confirmed the international community was informed. Benmehidi claimed no Gaddafi family members were subject to UN sanctions, a claim contradicted by UN Security Council Resolution 1970 (February 26), which includes the three children now in Algeria, subjecting them to a travel ban due to their association with the regime. This resolution requires member states to prevent their entry unless the council approves an exception. The resolution also allows a nation to determine, on a case-by-case basis, if entry is needed for peace and stability, requiring notification to the committee within 48 hours. Also on Monday, a senior rebel commander reported the death of Khamis Gaddafi, Muammar's son and military commander, in a battle between Tarhuna and Bani Walid. Mahdi al-Harati, the rebels' Military Council vice chairman, stated Khamis died of injuries sustained in the battle and was buried by rebel forces. Muammar Gaddafi remains wanted by the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague for war crimes, along with Saif al-Islam Gaddafi and Abdullah al-Sanussi.  Algeria, however, is not an ICC signatory. Gaddafi's whereabouts remain unknown since rebels seized Tripoli. The National Transitional Council (NTC), forming a provisional government, hasn't confirmed the news about Gaddafi's family, but spokesman Mahmoud al-Shammam stated that if true, the NTC would demand their return and a fair trial. Rebels suspected Gaddafi might try to reach Algeria or Chad. Britain's Foreign and Commonwealth Office stated the matter is for the NTC. The White House indicated no knowledge of Gaddafi leaving Libya. A senior Obama administration official, speaking anonymously, said Gaddafi's wife and children were likely in Algerian government custody. A State Department spokeswoman, Victoria Nuland, emphasized accountability for Gaddafi and his family members. Algeria's potential support for Gaddafi has been noted, given the similarities between their economies and governments, according to Jon Alterman of the Center for Strategic and International Studies. Aisha Gaddafi, formerly a UN Goodwill Ambassador, had her position terminated after the conflict began. Hannibal Gaddafi, known for his lavish spending and violent incidents, reportedly paid millions to entertainers and had a nanny badly burned by his wife, Aline Skaf. Mohamed Gaddafi, initially reported captured, later escaped. CNN's Jill Dougherty, Greg Botelho, Richard Roth, and Mohammed Tawfeeq contributed to this report.
translated_content: A esposa e três filhos do líder líbio foragido, Muammar Gaddafi, juntamente com alguns netos, chegaram à Argélia na manhã de segunda-feira, segundo diplomatas argelinos. Mourad Benmehidi, embaixador da Argélia na ONU, informou o secretário-geral da ONU, Ban Ki-moon. Benmehidi declarou que a Argélia concedeu entrada por 'motivos humanitários' a Safia, Aisha, Hannibal e Mohamed Gaddafi e seus filhos. Ele confirmou que a comunidade internacional foi informada. Benmehidi alegou que nenhum membro da família Gaddafi estava sujeito a sanções da ONU, afirmação contradita pela Resolução 1970 do Conselho de Segurança da ONU (26 de fevereiro), que inclui os três filhos agora na Argélia, sujeitando-os a uma proibição de viagem devido à sua associação com o regime. Essa resolução exige que os estados-membros impeçam sua entrada, a menos que o conselho aprove uma exceção. A resolução também permite que uma nação determine, caso a caso, se a entrada é necessária para a paz e a estabilidade, exigindo notificação ao comitê dentro de 48 horas. Também na segunda-feira, um comandante rebelde sênior relatou a morte de Khamis Gaddafi, filho e comandante militar de Muammar, em uma batalha entre Tarhuna e Bani Walid. Mahdi al-Harati, vice-presidente do Conselho Militar dos rebeldes, declarou que Khamis morreu de ferimentos sofridos na batalha e foi enterrado pelas forças rebeldes. Muammar Gaddafi continua procurado pelo Tribunal Penal Internacional (TPI) em Haia por crimes de guerra, juntamente com Saif al-Islam Gaddafi e Abdullah al-Sanussi.  A Argélia, porém, não é signatária do TPI. O paradeiro de Gaddafi permanece desconhecido desde que os rebeldes tomaram Tripoli. O Conselho Nacional de Transição (CNT), que forma um governo provisório, não confirmou as notícias sobre a família de Gaddafi, mas o porta-voz Mahmoud al-Shammam declarou que, se verdadeiro, o CNT exigiria seu retorno e um julgamento justo. Os rebeldes suspeitavam que Gaddafi pudesse tentar chegar à Argélia ou ao Chade. O Ministério das Relações Exteriores e da Commonwealth da Grã-Bretanha declarou que o assunto é de responsabilidade do CNT. A Casa Branca indicou não ter conhecimento de Gaddafi ter deixado a Líbia. Um funcionário sênior da administração Obama, falando anonimamente, disse que a esposa e os filhos de Gaddafi provavelmente estavam sob custódia do governo argelino. Uma porta-voz do Departamento de Estado, Victoria Nuland, enfatizou a responsabilização de Gaddafi e dos membros de sua família. O potencial apoio da Argélia a Gaddafi foi observado, dadas as semelhanças entre suas economias e governos, segundo Jon Alterman, do Centro de Estudos Estratégicos e Internacionais. Aisha Gaddafi, ex-embaixadora da boa vontade da ONU, teve seu cargo encerrado após o início do conflito. Hannibal Gaddafi, conhecido por seus gastos extravagantes e incidentes violentos, teria pago milhões a artistas e teve uma babá gravemente queimada por sua esposa, Aline Skaf. Mohamed Gaddafi, inicialmente relatado como capturado, escapou posteriormente. Jill Dougherty, Greg Botelho, Richard Roth e Mohammed Tawfeeq da CNN contribuíram para esta reportagem.
